title: The Walk to the Lake
premise: At daybreak a widow rises at 1906 Prairie, eight years after her husband walked out of this door at six in the morning and never came back. Retrace his last walk, from his brother's door to the lake.

opening.text:
JAUNT: THE WALK TO THE LAKE. Daybreak on a Monday in November 1904, at the south end of Prairie Avenue.

Four stops, north along Prairie toward the lake. The Keiths are the steadiest family on the street: three brothers, three houses, one great wholesale firm. But one Monday morning eight years ago, at about this hour, the gentlest of them got up after a sleepless night, put on his hat and coat, and walked out of his front door. He walked.

Start at his door, where his widow still lives.

stops.text: 1906 Prairie, at daybreak. The widow here is Mrs. Edson Keith. Eight years ago her husband, Edson, a merchant, "disappeared from his home at 1906 Prairie avenue about 6 o'clock in the morning". He was 63 and had come to Chicago in 1854. For at least ten years he had barely slept. That last night he paced the halls again, and "his butler found him in a state of deliriousness at 2 AM". By six he was gone. Hilda Johnson, the ladies' maid, is first up; Paul Rasmussen, the coachman, is crossing the yard. Mrs. Keith comes to the door to look at the weather. Walk north to the brother's house next door.

stage.caption: Mrs. Edson Keith opens her door at first light and looks up the street toward the lake; her maid stands behind her.

stops.text: 1900 Prairie, the house of his brother Elbridge, built in 1870 in the Second Empire style that once ruled this street. Elbridge and his wife saw it coming. A few weeks before that Monday they spoke with Edson's wife, and she told them, "I … suspect that he was losing control of his mind through long suffering." His personal secretary said he had never heard him say anything nasty or unkind about anyone. That was Edson Keith: the gentle brother, the one who never raised his voice. Elbridge is up early this morning too, and he still passes his brother's door. Walk north up Prairie, the way Edson went.

stage.caption: Elbridge Keith comes down his steps in the half light, and his wife watches him go from the door.

stops.text: 1808 Prairie, the Osborn R. Keith house. He and Albert Faxon founded the family firm on Lake Street in 1858, and by the 1880s Edson Keith & Company was selling $4.5 million a year, with two hundred people in Chicago and five hundred more in a Milwaukee factory. Three Keith houses on one street, and a fortune. In 1904 the house is Stanley Field's, but the street still calls it a Keith house. Edson walked past it in the dark that Monday, going north, toward the lake. It is a long walk for a sick man. The house will be razed in 1968, all but the north wall that screens the Glessner courtyard. Keep going north to Sixteenth Street.

stage.caption: A milkman's boy runs the morning round past 1808, the only other soul on the street.

cast.name: An errand boy on the morning round (unnamed)

stops.text: Sixteenth Street, at the north end of the avenue. East of here, past the railroad, is the lake. This is as far as the street goes. Edson Keith went on. On the beach that Monday morning someone found a hat and a coat. Fishermen on the beach told what they had seen. The papers do not agree where: one says the foot of Sixteenth Street, another the foot of Thirteenth. All day Monday they searched. The servants worked it out only on Tuesday, when they read it in the newspaper. Stand here and look east at first light. The lake is grey and flat and very large, and it has never given back anything it did not want to.

stage.caption: A lone gentleman in a hat and coat walks east along Sixteenth Street toward the lake and does not look back.

cast.name: A gentleman walking east (unnamed; not Edson Keith, who died in 1896)

legs.story: North two doors, as he went, to his brother Elbridge's house.
North up Prairie Avenue in the half light, past the houses of the old firm.
North all the way to Sixteenth Street, the long walk toward the lake.

endings.text: End of the walk. The news came to the family "with paralyzing suddenness", and the dispatch reported that "the lake is now being dragged for the recovery of the remains." Edson Keith had made his will the year before, leaving $300,000 each to his wife Susan and their two sons. His wife stayed on at 1906 Prairie, and his brother next door. The street remembers him as the gentle brother, the one who never said an unkind word about anyone, who walked out of his own front door at six one Monday morning and went to the lake.

keepsake.title: The Keith Brothers
keepsake.text: An interpretive card of the Keith households of Prairie Avenue in 1904, not a historical artifact.

evidence.text: Edson Keith 'disappeared from his home at 1906 Prairie avenue about 6 o'clock in the morning' of Monday 21 September 1896; the Argus report put the place at the lake 'at the foot of Thirteenth street', and 'search was made for the missing man all day Monday'. 'He was 63 years old and came to Chicago in 1854.'

He had spent another sleepless night pacing the hallways of his home, and his butler found him in a state of deliriousness at 2 AM. A hat and coat were found on the beach on Monday morning, and only when the household staff read the Tuesday newspaper did they realise what had happened. Fishermen on the beach told what they had seen.
evidence.locator: The post's second to fourth paragraphs.

evidence.text: Edson Keith, merchant, sleepless and ill for at least a decade, left his house early on Monday 21 September 1896, walked to the lake at the foot of 16th Street and drowned; the papers said he 'committed suicide Monday morning by drowning himself in Lake Michigan'.
evidence.locator: The account of his death, from the Tribune and Chronicle of September 1896.

evidence.text: The Edson Keith who drowned in 1896 is the late husband of the Mrs. Edson Keith at 1906 Prairie.
evidence.reasoning: A Chicago merchant Edson Keith died in 1896, leaving a widow; in 1900 and 1904 a widowed Mrs. Edson Keith keeps house at 1906 Prairie, beside Elbridge G. Keith at 1900, and the ghost tours call the drowned man Elbridge's brother. No source read here states the identity in one sentence.

evidence.text: The 1904 Blue Book lists Elbridge G. Keith at 1900 Prairie and Mrs. Edson Keith at 1906; the 1900 census gives Mrs. Edson Keith as widowed.
evidence.locator: The street-and-number list, PRAIRIE AV., as data/residents_1904/households/hh_keith_elbridge_g.json and hh_keith_mrs_edson.json read it; ED 40, sheet 4B, line 95.

evidence.text: The census of 1 June 1900 enumerated Paul Rasmussen, coachman, born in Denmark, as the head of his own household in the rear building behind 1906 Prairie.

The Walk to the Lake: the day, Monday 21 November 1904, the hour and the order of the walk are this jaunt's framing, chosen because the stories meet on it (three days after Arthur Caton's death, a Monday of the Reading Class, before Kimball's death in December). No visit on that day is asserted.

The Walk to the Lake: who is seen at each stop, where they stand, what they do and when are reconstructed. People with cards in the town play themselves; people the town has no card for (and the unnamed servants, callers and passers-by) are unnamed figures in period dress, and no likeness is claimed. No word anyone says is asserted.
His brother Elbridge and his wife had spoken with Mrs. Keith a few weeks before, and she had said, 'I … suspect that he was losing control of his mind through long suffering.'

His personal secretary said he had never heard him say anything nasty or unkind about anyone. The firm, founded in 1858 by Osborn R. Keith and Albert Faxon on Lake Street, had become Edson Keith & Company, with annual sales of $4.5 million in the mid-1880s, over 200 employees in Chicago and 500 more in a Milwaukee factory.
evidence.locator: The post's seventh to ninth paragraphs.

evidence.text: Elbridge G. Keith Residence. Built 1870; John W. Roberts, architect. The last surviving example of the popular Second Empire style, which dominated the street by the 1880s.
The 1904 Blue Book lists Mr. and Mrs. Stanley Field at 1808 Prairie.
evidence.locator: Prairie Av. street list, the 1808 line.

evidence.text: Osborn R. Keith Residence, 1808 S. Prairie Avenue: the north wall was retained during demolition in 1968 to preserve the private courtyard of the adjacent Glessner house.
His will of 13 March 1895 left $300,000 each to his wife Susan and to his two sons, Edson, Jr. and Walter W.
